core.text: The last and smallest noun family runs on *e*: **a 5th-declension noun (the e-pattern: dies, diei; res, rei)**. *diēs* (day): *diēs, diem, diēī, diēī, diē*; plural *diēs, diēs, diērum, diēbus, diēbus*. The two words that matter are *diēs* and *rēs* (thing, matter); the others are *faciēs* (face), *merīdiēs* (midday), *spēs* (hope), *fidēs* (trust), *glaciēs* (ice). They are feminine — except *diēs* and *merīdiēs*, which are masculine. Latin name: dēclīnātiō quīnta.
A declension is a family of nouns that share one set of endings. This is the fifth and last: after it there are no more noun patterns to learn.
-ēs, -em, -ēī, -ēī, -ē; plural -ēs, -ēs, -ērum, -ēbus, -ēbus; the genitive -ēī marks the family.

invented.en: In summer the days are long.

core.text: *diēs* and *rēs* look like 3rd-declension plurals (*ovēs*, *pānēs*). The dictionary genitive tells them apart: *diēs, diēī* (5th) against *ovis, ovis* (3rd). In a sentence, an *-ēs* form with a singular verb (*diēs est*) is a 5th-declension singular; and only the 5th has *-ēī, -ērum, -ēbus*.

teach.title: What it does
teach.say: One noun family is left, and it is the smallest: **a 5th-declension noun (the e-pattern: diēs, diēī; rēs, reī)**. Its endings run on *e* the way the first family runs on *a* and the second on *o*. At this point in the book it holds *diēs* (day), *merīdiēs* (midday), *faciēs* (face) and *glaciēs* (ice).

check.ask: Which word here is the 5th-declension noun?

teach.title: Subject -ēs, object -em
teach.say: One cell at a time. The nominative (the subject form) ends in *-ēs*: *diēs*, *faciēs*. The accusative (the object form) ends in *-em*: *diem*, *faciem*. Only the last syllable changes.

show.say: diēs / diem — only the last syllable changes

check.ask: Fill the subject cell and the object cell of *diēs*.

teach.title: The genitive and dative -ēī
teach.say: Two cells that are spelt alike. The genitive (the 'of' form) and the dative (the 'to/for' form) are both *-ēī*: *diēī*, of the day or to the day; *faciēī*. Both of the nouns you have met keep the long *-ēī*, because their stem ends in a vowel; one whose stem ends in a consonant shortens it to *-eī* (*rēs, reī*), and you meet none of those yet. In practice you will meet the genitive far more often than the dative: *initium diēī*, the beginning of the day.

show.say: diēī / diēī — the 'of' cell and the 'to/for' cell are spelt alike

check.ask: Fill the genitive (the 'of' form) and the dative (the 'to/for' form) of *diēs*. They are the same spelling.

teach.title: The ablative -ē and the plural
teach.say: The ablative (the 'by/with/from' form) is a bare long *-ē*: *diē*, *merīdiē*. In the plural the subject and object are *-ēs* again, the genitive is *-ērum* (*diērum*) and the dative and ablative *-ēbus* (*diēbus*).

show.say: diē, diērum, diēbus — a bare long -ē, then the two plural endings

check.ask: Give the ablative singular of *diēs*, then its genitive plural and its dative plural.

teach.title: Telling it from a 3rd-declension -ēs
teach.say: *Diēs* looks exactly like *nūbēs* (a cloud) and *vallēs* (a valley) — but those are 3rd declension, and each of them spells its plural exactly like its singular. Two tests. The dictionary genitive: *diēs, diēī* against *nūbēs, nūbis*. And the verb: *diēs obscūrus est* is singular, *nūbēs multae sunt* is plural.

check.ask: *Vallēs* and *diēs* both end in *-ēs*. Which one is 5th declension, and what settles it?

teach.title: Using it: which gender?
teach.say: The family is feminine — *faciēs pulchra*, *glaciēs frīgida* — but the two day-words are masculine: *diēs* and *merīdiēs*. So *hic diēs longus*, *diēs longī*, and *merīdiēs calidus*, never *merīdiēs calida*. Get the gender right and the adjective follows.

check.ask: Faciēs Aemiliae ___ et laeta est. *faciēs* is feminine. (pulcher)

more.text: Only *diēs* and *rēs* have a full plural; most of the others are used in the singular. After a consonant the *-ēī* shortens to *-eī*: *reī, speī, fideī*. *Rēs* is everywhere in idioms: *rēs pūblica* (the state), *rē vērā* (in truth), *quā dē rē* (about which matter).
*diēs* is masculine when it means a day in general, feminine when it means a fixed date or a stretch of time: *diē certā* — on the appointed day. *merīdiēs* is always masculine.

The learner's notes (week 13): in every case but the genitive the pattern matches the *is*-nouns with *e* where they have *e* or *i* (*diēs, diem, diēbus*); the genitive looks like the 2nd declension with an *e* in front (*-eī, -ērum*). Ørberg (chapter XIII) declines *diēs* and adds *merīdiēs* m., *faciēs* and *glaciēs* f. and a few other feminines; *māne* (morning) is an indeclinable neuter that never changes its ending.
